records.prompt: Each section of equipment that requires rear or side access to make field connections shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the ___.
records.gist: Some equipment requires rear or side access for field connections. The manufacturer must mark it where visible before the enclosure is opened. The question asks where that mark goes.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 408.18(C), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
'Listed' means an independent lab tested it for one specific purpose — use it only that way and follow its instructions, because the instructions are part of the listing. Novelty and special equipment (USB cover plates with night lights, holiday lighting) must be listed, and required markings must be durable and visible where the inspector and the user will actually see them.

This asks about a required marking or label. Decide what must be marked, where the marking goes, and what it must say — the answer is the location or wording the NEC specifies.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
408.18(C) Connections
Each section of equipment that requires rear or side access to make field connections shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the front. Section openings requiring rear or side access shall comply with 110.26. Load terminals for field wiring shall comply with 408.18(C)(1), (C)(2), or (C)(3) as applicable.
(1) Equipment Grounding Conductors
Load terminals for field wiring shall be so located that it is not necessary to reach across uninsulated ungrounded bus in order to make connections.
(2) Grounded Circuit Conductors
Where multiple branch or feeder grounded circuit conductor load terminals for field wiring are grouped together in one location, they shall be so located that it is not necessary to reach across uninsulated ungrounded bus, whether or not energized, in order to make connections.
records.tip_short: Rear or side field connections get a marking on the front, where the installer looks first. Correct: A — front. 408.18(C) says sections needing rear or side access shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the front. Not B: The right side is not where 408.18(C) puts the marking; it must be on the front. Not C: The left side is not where 408.18(C) puts the marking; it must be on the front. Not D: A rear marking is only found after walking around; 408.18(C) requires the marking on the front.
choice_notes: 408.18(C) says sections needing rear or side access shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the front.
The right side is not where 408.18(C) puts the marking; it must be on the front.
The left side is not where 408.18(C) puts the marking; it must be on the front.
A rear marking is only found after walking around; 408.18(C) requires the marking on the front.

records.prompt: Disregarding demand factors, the calculated lighting load for a 5,000 sq. ft. office building is ___ volt-amperes.
records.gist: Office occupancies use a fixed volt-ampere value per square foot of floor area. The question hands you 5,000 square feet and says to skip the demand math. Multiply and pick the total.
records.article_title: Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: load calculation. Start with Table 220.42(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This is a load-calculation question. Numbers in the question: 5,000 sq. ft. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

Type of Occupancy	Volt-amperes/m²	Volt-amperes/ft²
Office	14	1.3
Note: The 125 percent multiplier for a continuous load as specified in 210.20(A) is included, therefore no additional multiplier shall be required when using the unit loads in this table for calculating the minimum lighting load for a specified occupancy.

Not B: 15,400 VA implies about 3.1 VA per square foot; Table 220.42(A) lists offices at only 1.3 VA. records.reference_text:
310.6(C) Ungrounded Conductors
Conductors that are intended for use as ungrounded conductors, whether used as a single conductor or in multiconductor cables, shall be finished to be clearly distinguishable from grounded conductors and equipment grounding conductors. Distinguishing markings shall not conflict in any manner with the surface markings required by 310.8(B)(1). Branch-circuit ungrounded conductors shall be identified in accordance with 210.5(C). Feeders shall be identified in accordance with 215.12(C).
Exception: Conductor identification shall be permitted in accordance with 200.7.
records.tip_short: Hot conductors may be any color except white, gray, or green, which are reserved for neutral and ground. Correct: C — pink. Pink is not white, gray, or green, so it is clearly distinguishable from grounded and grounding conductors. Not A: Green is reserved for equipment grounding conductors, so it cannot identify an ungrounded conductor. Not B: Gray identifies a grounded conductor, so an ungrounded conductor must be distinguishable from it. Not D: White identifies a grounded (neutral) conductor, so it cannot be the ungrounded conductor color.

records.reference_text:
220.14(H) Fixed Multioutlet Assemblies
Fixed multioutlet assemblies used in other than dwelling units or the guest rooms or guest suites of hotels or motels shall be calculated in accordance with the following:
(1) Where appliances are unlikely to be used simultaneously, each 1.5 m (5 ft) or fraction thereof of each separate and continuous length shall be considered as one outlet of not less than 180 volt-amperes.
(2) Where appliances are likely to be used simultaneously, each 300 mm (1 ft) or fraction thereof shall be considered as an outlet of not less than 180 volt-amperes.
For the purposes of this section, the calculation shall be permitted to be based on the portion that contains receptacles.
records.tip_short: Appliances not used at once: each 5 feet or fraction of multioutlet assembly counts as one 180 VA outlet. Correct: C — 540. 220.14(H) counts each 5 feet or fraction as one 180 VA outlet, so 12 feet is 3 times 180, or 540 VA. Not A: 1,000 VA does not come from the 180 VA per 5 feet rule; 12 feet gives 3 outlets, or 540 VA. Not B: 720 VA counts 4 outlets, but 12 feet is only three 5 foot sections (two full plus a fraction). Not D: 380 VA is about 2 outlets; the leftover 2 foot fraction also counts, so 3 times 180 VA is 540 VA.
records.formula: Not simultaneous: one 180 VA outlet per 5 ft or fraction (220.14(H)(1)). Count the outlets first.

records.prompt: In a dwelling bedroom, any wall space ___ or more in width (including space measured around corners) and unbroken along the floor line by doorways and similar openings, fireplaces, and fixed cabinets that do not have countertops or similar work surfaces.
records.gist: Dwelling bedroom walls require receptacles at defined spacing, and only qualifying wall segments count toward it. The question asks how wide a stretch has to be before it counts.
records.article_title: Branch Circuits Not Over 1000 Volts AC, 1500 Volts DC, Nominal
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: dwelling unit. Start with 210.52(A)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

In plain terms, the question is: "In a dwelling bedroom, any wall space ___ or more in width (including space measured around corners) and unbroken along the floor…" Subject: dwelling unit. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS

records.reference_text:
210.52(A)(2) Wall Space
As used in this section, a wall space shall include the following:
Any space 600 mm (2 ft) or more in width (including space measured around corners) and unbroken along the floor line by doorways and similar openings, fireplaces, stationary appliances, and fixed cabinets that do not have countertops or similar work surfaces
The space occupied by fixed panels in walls, excluding sliding panels
The space afforded by fixed room dividers, such as freestanding bar-type counters or railings

Not A: 18 inches is too short; 210.52(A)(2) counts wall space of 600 mm (2 feet), or 24 inches, and wider. Not C: 30 inches is not the threshold; wall space begins at 2 feet, which is 24 inches. Not D: 36 inches is not the threshold; 210.52(A)(2) counts spaces 2 feet (24 inches) or wider.

210.8(A) Dwelling Units
All 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles installed in the following locations and supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground shall have ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel:
(1) Bathrooms
(2) Garages and also accessory buildings that have a floor located at or below grade level not intended as habitable rooms and limited to storage areas, work areas, and areas of similar use
(3) Outdoors
(4) Crawl spaces - at or below grade level
(5) Basements
(6) Kitchens

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

In plain terms, the question is: "If festoon lighting is installed without a messenger, the smallest allowable overhead conductor is ___ AWG." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

records.reference_text:
225.6(B) Festoon Lighting
Overhead conductors for festoon lighting shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless the conductors are supported by messenger wires. In all spans exceeding 12 m (40 ft), the conductors shall be supported by messenger wire. The messenger wire shall be supported by strain insulators. Conductors or messenger wires shall not be attached to any fire escape, downspout, or plumbing equipment.
records.tip_short: Festoon lighting without a messenger: 12 AWG minimum; any span over 40 feet always needs a messenger. Correct: B — #12. 225.6(B) says festoon conductors shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless supported by messenger wire. Not A: #10 is allowed but is not the smallest; 225.6(B) permits down to 12 AWG without a messenger. Not C: #14 is smaller than the 12 AWG minimum 225.6(B) sets for festoon conductors without a messenger. Not D: #16 is far below the 12 AWG minimum for unsupported overhead festoon conductors.
choice_notes: #10 is allowed but is not the smallest; 225.6(B) permits down to 12 AWG without a messenger.
225.6(B) says festoon conductors shall not be smaller than 12 AWG unless supported by messenger wire.

records.prompt: For temporary holiday lighting, trees shall be permitted for supporting overhead spans of conductors and cables if the overhead wiring is arranged with ___, tension take-up devices, or other approved means to avoid damage from live vegetation.
records.gist: Vegetation moves with growth and wind, so outdoor wiring on trees requires flexible attachment means. The question asks what that hardware is called.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable, conductors, temporary wiring. Start with 590.4(J), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Luminaires (fixtures) follow one idea: bulbs get hot and breakable, so guard them — temporary job-site lamps need a guard or proper holder, and holiday/decorative lighting must be listed. Fluorescent and LED fixtures with serviceable ballasts or drivers in commercial buildings need their own disconnect so relamping doesn't happen live. Outdoors, keep fixtures and their wiring away from power lines and support festoon spans so plants and weather can't damage them.

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Subject: holiday lighting. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
cable, conductors, temporary wiring
records.reference_text:
590.4(J) Support
Exception: For holiday lighting in accordance with 590.3(B), where the conductors or cables are arranged with strain relief devices, tension take-up devices, or other approved means to avoid damage from the movement of the live vegetation, trees shall be permitted to be used for support of overhead spans of branch-circuit conductors or cables.

The 590.4(J) exception allows tree support where wiring has strain relief or tension take-up devices. Not A: Fittings are not named in 590.4(J); the exception lists strain relief or tension take-up devices. records.prompt: Duty on elevator and dumbwaiter driving machine motors and driving motors of motor-generators used with generator field control shall be rated as ___.
records.gist: An elevator motor draws high current briefly and then rests, unlike continuous-duty loads. The question asks what the Code calls that kind of work cycle.
records.article_title: Elevators, Dumbwaiters, Escalators, Moving Walks, Platform Lifts, and Stairway Chairlifts
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor. Start with 620.61(B)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Elevator and dumbwaiter motors live an intermittent life — short hard runs, long rests — so the Code sizes their conductors and protection by duty rating instead of continuous-duty rules. Their machine rooms and controllers get the same disconnect-within-sight treatment as any motor.

This asks you to match this motor or transformer setup to its rule. Subject: motor. Identify whether the question is about protection size, conductor size, disconnect location, or marking.

records.reference_text:
620.61(B)(1) Duty Rating on Elevator, Dumbwaiter, and Motor-Generator Sets Driving Motors
Duty on elevator and dumbwaiter driving machine motors and driving motors of motor-generators used with generator field control shall be rated as intermittent. Such motors shall be permitted to be protected against overload in accordance with 430.33.

Correct: A — intermittent. 620.61(B)(1) says these driving motors shall be rated as intermittent duty. Not B: Lockable describes a disconnecting means feature, not a motor duty rating. Not C: Continuous duty means running steadily; elevator motors start and stop, so the Code says intermittent. Not D: Varying duty is a different duty class; 620.61(B)(1) specifically requires intermittent.

records.prompt: What does the alpha character I represent when stating the question W = E x I?
records.gist: Power in watts is the product of volts and a second quantity represented by the letter I. The question asks what I stands for.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

In plain terms, the question is: "What does the alpha character I represent when stating the question W = E x I?" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Power Equation (Watt's Law)
In the electrical power equation W = E x I (Watts = Volts x Amperes), the letter I traditionally designates 'Intensity of current' (from the French 'intensité du courant'), representing current flow in amperes.
records.tip_short: In W = E x I, the I stands for intensity of current, measured in amperes. Correct: C — Intensity of current. I stands for intensity of current, the current flow measured in amperes. Not A: Intrinsic circuit is not an electrical variable; I in the power formula is current in amperes. Not B: Electromotive force is the E (volts) in W = E x I, not the I. Not D: Isotopic character is a chemistry idea, unrelated to the current variable I.
choice_notes: Intrinsic circuit is not an electrical variable; I in the power formula is current in amperes.
Electromotive force is the E (volts) in W = E x I, not the I.
I stands for intensity of current, the current flow measured in amperes.
Isotopic character is a chemistry idea, unrelated to the current variable I.

records.prompt: Where multiple driven ground rods are used to form the grounding electrode system, in order to maintain an effective grounding electrode system, they shall not be less than ___ apart.
records.gist: Two ground rods installed too close together function as a single electrode. The question asks how far apart they must stand so both actually work.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounding electrode. Start with 250.53(A)(3), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: grounding electrode. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
grounding electrode
records.reference_text:
250.53(A)(3) Supplemental Electrode
If multiple rod, pipe, or plate electrodes are installed to meet the requirements of this section, they shall not be less than 1.8 m (6 ft) apart.
Informational Note: The paralleling efficiency of rods is increased by spacing them twice the length of the longest rod.
records.tip_short: Multiple ground rods go at least 6 feet (72 inches) apart; twice the rod length works even better. Correct: D — 72 inches. 250.53(A)(3) requires rods at least 1.8 m (6 feet) apart, and 6 feet is 72 inches. Not A: 36 inches is only half enough; 250.53(A)(3) requires at least 1.8 m (6 feet), which is 72 inches. Not B: 48 inches is too close; the rods must be at least 6 feet, or 72 inches, apart. Not C: 60 inches is too close; 250.53(A)(3) requires at least 6 feet, which is 72 inches.
choice_notes: 36 inches is only half enough; 250.53(A)(3) requires at least 1.8 m (6 feet), which is 72 inches.
48 inches is too close; the rods must be at least 6 feet, or 72 inches, apart.
60 inches is too close; 250.53(A)(3) requires at least 6 feet, which is 72 inches.
250.53(A)(3) requires rods at least 1.8 m (6 feet) apart, and 6 feet is 72 inches.

records.prompt: All 15 or 20 amp, single-phase, 125 volt through 250 volt receptacles located within ___ feet of a fountain edge shall be provided with GFCI protection.
records.gist: A fountain places water and people together, so nearby receptacles require ground-fault protection. The question asks how far from the water's edge that rule reaches.
records.article_title: Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground-fault circuit-interrupter, receptacle outlet. Start with 680.58, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

This asks where GFCI protection is required. Subject: receptacle. Numbers in the question: 20 amp, 125 volt, 250 volt. Match the location and equipment in the question to the list of places the NEC names.

LOOKUP FOCUS
ground-fault circuit-interrupter, receptacle outlet
records.reference_text:
680.58 Ground-Fault Circuit-Interrupter (GFCI) and Special Purpose Ground-Fault Circuit-Interrupter (SPGFCI) Protection for Adjacent Receptacle Outlets
All receptacles rated 125 volts through 250 volts, 60 amperes or less, located within 6.0 m (20 ft) of a fountain edge shall have GFCI protection complying with 680.5(B) or SPGFCI protection complying with 680.5(C), as applicable.

Not C: 25 feet is not the fountain rule; 680.58 uses 6.0 m (20 feet). Not D: 30 feet is not the fountain rule; 680.58 requires GFCI within 20 feet of the edge.
choice_notes: 680.58 requires GFCI for receptacles located within 6.0 m (20 feet) of a fountain edge.
24 feet is not in 680.58; the GFCI distance from a fountain edge is 20 feet.
25 feet is not the fountain rule; 680.58 uses 6.0 m (20 feet).

records.prompt: The ampacity of three #10 THWN-2 conductors installed in a raceway is ___ amps if the ambient temperature is 112°F.
records.gist: Elevated ambient temperature reduces conductor ampacity; apply the temperature correction factor to the table value. Three of these wires at 112 degrees. The question asks what each one is still good for.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, raceway, conductors. Start with Table 310.15(B)(1)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). FMC = Flexible Metal Conduit (bendable whip). ENT = Electrical Nonmetallic Tubing (blue smurf tube). LFMC = Liquidtight Flexible Metal (sealed whip). RNC = Rigid Nonmetallic Conduit (PVC). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

records.prompt: Fuel dispensing systems shall be provided with one or more clearly identified emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects. Such disconnects or devices shall be installed in approved locations but not less than 20 feet or more than ___ feet from the fuel dispensing devices that they serve.
records.gist: Fuel dispensing areas require an emergency shutoff that is reachable during a fire yet positioned away from the hazard. Twenty feet is given as the near limit. The question asks the far limit.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: disconnecting means. Start with 514.11(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A disconnecting means is simply the switch or breaker a worker opens before touching equipment. The golden rule is 'within sight': visible and no more than 50 ft away, so nobody can re-energize it unseen. Motors need a disconnect in sight of both the controller and the motor itself; appliances and AC units need one in sight and quickly reachable. If the disconnect must live far away, it has to be lockable open with the location marked on the equipment.

This is a maximum-limit question. Numbers in the question: 20 feet. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
514.11(A) Emergency Electrical Disconnects
Fuel dispensing systems shall be provided with one or more clearly identified emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects. Such devices or disconnects shall be installed in approved locations but not less than 6 m (20 ft) or more than 30 m (100 ft) from the fuel dispensing devices that they serve. Emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects shall disconnect power to all dispensing devices; to all remote pumps serving the dispensing devices; to all associated power, control, and signal circuits; and to all other electrical equipment in the hazardous (classified) locations surrounding the fuel dispensing devices. When more than one emergency shutoff device or electrical disconnect is provided, all devices shall be interconnected. Resetting from an emergency shutoff condition shall require manual intervention and the manner of resetting shall be approved by the authority having jurisdiction. [30A:6.7] The emergency shutoff device shall disconnect simultaneously from the source of supply, all conductors of the circuits, including the grounded conductor, if any. Equipment grounding conductors shall remain connected.
records.tip_short: Fuel dispenser emergency shutoff: at least 20 feet but no more than 100 feet from the dispensers. Correct: D — 100. 514.11(A) requires the shutoff not less than 20 feet or more than 30 m (100 feet) from the dispensers. Not A: 50 feet is within range but is not the maximum; 514.11(A) allows up to 30 m (100 feet). Not B: 75 feet is not the limit; 514.11(A) sets the maximum at 30 m (100 feet). Not C: 80 feet is not the limit; the maximum distance in 514.11(A) is 100 feet.
choice_notes: 50 feet is within range but is not the maximum; 514.11(A) allows up to 30 m (100 feet).
75 feet is not the limit; 514.11(A) sets the maximum at 30 m (100 feet).
80 feet is not the limit; the maximum distance in 514.11(A) is 100 feet.
514.11(A) requires the shutoff not less than 20 feet or more than 30 m (100 feet) from the dispensers.

records.prompt: Where conduits enter a floor-standing switchboard, switchgear, or panelboard at the bottom, the conduits, including their end fittings, shall not rise more than ___ inches above the bottom of the enclosure.
records.gist: Raceways entering the bottom of floor-standing equipment cannot extend so far inside that they interfere with internal components. The question asks how many inches above the bottom they may rise.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit. Start with 408.5, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

Where conduits or other raceways enter a switchboard, switchgear, floor-standing panelboard, or similar enclosure at the bottom, approved space shall be provided to permit installation of conductors in the enclosure. The wiring space shall not be less than shown in Table 408.5 where the conduit or raceways enter or leave the enclosure below the busbars, their supports, or other obstructions. records.prompt: Thermostatically controlled switching devices serving as both controllers and disconnecting means for fixed electric space heating equipment shall ___.
answers: be located not more than 8 feet above floor level
open all grounded conductors when placed in the off position
be designed so that the circuit cannot be energized automatically after the device has been manually placed in the off position
records.gist: A thermostat may serve as the disconnect only with a maintained OFF position requiring manual reset. The question asks what the Code demands of that switch.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounded conductor, conductors, disconnecting means. Start with 424.20(A)(3), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

This asks about the disconnect for this equipment. Subject: disconnecting means. Decide whether the question wants its location, its height, its rating, or who may access it.

LOOKUP FOCUS
grounded conductor, conductors, disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
424.20(A) Serving as Both Controllers and Disconnecting Means
Thermostatically controlled switching devices and combination thermostats and manually controlled switches shall be permitted to serve as both controllers and disconnecting means, provided they meet all of the following conditions:
Provided with a marked "off" position
Directly open all ungrounded conductors when manually placed in the "off" position
Designed so that the circuit cannot be energized automatically after the device has been manually placed in the "off" position
Located as specified in 424.19
Located in an accessible location
records.tip_short: A thermostat used as a heater disconnect must stay off once manually set to off, and open all hot conductors. Correct: D — be designed so that the circuit cannot be energized automatically after the device has been manually placed in the off position. 424.20(A) requires that the circuit cannot energize automatically after being manually placed off. Not A: 424.20(A) expressly permits thermostats to serve as both controller and disconnecting means. Not B: 424.20(A) sets no 8 foot height limit; the device must be located per 424.19 and be accessible. Not C: 424.20(A) requires opening all ungrounded conductors, not the grounded conductors.
choice_notes: 424.20(A) expressly permits thermostats to serve as both controller and disconnecting means.
424.20(A) sets no 8 foot height limit; the device must be located per 424.19 and be accessible.
424.20(A) requires opening all ungrounded conductors, not the grounded conductors.
424.20(A) requires that the circuit cannot energize automatically after being manually placed off.

records.prompt: For a feeder tap not exceeding 10 feet in length and field installation, the maximum overcurrent device rating supplying a tap conductor with an ampacity of 40 amps is ___.
records.gist: A small tap conductor off a larger feeder has no overcurrent protection of its own, so the Code limits the rating of the upstream feeder overcurrent device. A 40-amp tap is given. The question asks that cap.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: feeder, ampacity, overcurrent protection. Start with 240.21(B)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: feeder. Numbers in the question: 10 feet, 40 amps. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
feeder, ampacity, overcurrent protection
records.reference_text:
240.21(B)(1) Taps Not Over 3 m (10 ft) Long
If the length of the tap conductors does not exceed 3 m (10 ft) and the tap conductors comply with all of the following:
(1) The ampacity of the tap conductors is as follows:
a. Not less than the combined calculated loads on the circuits supplied by the tap conductors
b. Not less than the rating of the equipment containing an overcurrent device(s) supplied by the tap conductors or not less than the rating of the overcurrent protective device at the termination of the tap conductors
(2) The tap conductors do not extend beyond the switchboard, switchgear, panelboard, disconnecting means, or control devices they supply.
(3) Except at the point of connection to the feeder, the tap conductors are enclosed in a raceway, which extends from the tap to the enclosure of an enclosed switchboard, switchgear, a panelboard, or control devices, or to the back of an open switchboard.
(4) For field installations, if the tap conductors leave the enclosure or vault in which the tap is made, the ampacity of the tap conductors is not less than one-tenth of the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder conductors.
Informational Note: See 408.36 for overcurrent protection requirements for panelboards.
records.tip_short: 10 foot field tap leaving the enclosure: tap ampacity at least one-tenth of the feeder breaker, so 40 x 10. A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. A stop pushbutton switch has normally closed (NC) contacts that must open the control circuit to de-energize the magnetic holding coil. Therefore, the stop switch is always wired in series with the motor control circuit.

records.prompt: Communications wires and cables and CATV type coaxial cables shall have a vertical clearance of not less than ___ from all points of roofs above which they pass.
records.gist: Communications conductors crossing over a roof must maintain clearance above the roof surface. The question asks that minimum height.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable. Start with 800.44(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Beyond ordinary wire-in-conduit, the NEC gives each special system its own article: flat FCC/FC cables glued under carpet squares, busways and cablebus feeding big loads, wireways and auxiliary gutters as roomy sheet-metal raceways (mind the spacing between live parts), and surface extensions for remodels. Questions on these almost always ask where the system is allowed, how it attaches, or what it must be marked.

This is a minimum-limit question. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
cable
records.reference_text:
800.44(B) Above Roofs
Communications wires and cables and CATV-type coaxial cables shall have a vertical clearance of not less than 2.5 m (8 ft) from all points of roofs above which they pass.
Exception No. 1: Communications wires and cables and CATV-type coaxial cables shall not be required to have a vertical clearance of not less than 2.5 m (8 ft) above auxiliary buildings, such as garages and the like.
Exception No. 2: A reduction in clearance above only the overhanging portion of the roof to not less than 450 mm (18 in.) shall be permitted if (1) not more than 1.2 m (4 ft) of communications and CATV-type service-drop conductors pass above the roof overhang and (2) they are terminated at a through- or above-the-roof raceway or approved support.
Exception No. 3: Where the roof has a slope of not less than 100 mm in 300 mm (4 in. in 12 in.), a reduction in clearance to not less than 900 mm (3 ft) shall be permitted.
records.tip_short: Communications cables over roofs need 8 feet of clearance; exceptions allow 18 inches over a short overhang or 3 feet on a steep roof. Correct: D — 8 feet. 800.44(B) requires not less than 2.5 m (8 feet) of vertical clearance from all points of roofs. Not A: 18 inches applies only to the roof overhang exception; the general clearance is 2.5 m (8 feet). Not B: 36 inches applies only under the 800.44(B) exception for roofs sloped at least 4 in. in 12 in.; the general clearance above roofs is 2.5 m (8 feet). Not C: 6 feet is too low; 800.44(B) requires 2.5 m (8 feet) above roofs.
choice_notes: 18 inches applies only to the roof overhang exception; the general clearance is 2.5 m (8 feet).
36 inches applies only under the 800.44(B) exception for roofs sloped at least 4 in. in 12 in.; the general clearance above roofs is 2.5 m (8 feet).
6 feet is too low; 800.44(B) requires 2.5 m (8 feet) above roofs.
800.44(B) requires not less than 2.5 m (8 feet) of vertical clearance from all points of roofs.

records.prompt: The maximum ampere rating permitted for a 125 volt, single-phase receptacle outlet having a cord-and-plug connected motor load that does not have individual overload protection is ___.
records.gist: A receptacle supplying a small motor without integral overload protection is limited in rating so a stalled motor cannot overheat the cord. The question asks the biggest outlet allowed there.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: switch ampere rating, receptacle outlet, motor, load calculation. Start with 430.42(C), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: receptacle. Numbers in the question: 125 volt. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
switch ampere rating, receptacle outlet, motor, load calculation
records.reference_text:
430.42(C) Cord-and-Plug-Connected
Where a motor is connected to a branch circuit by means of an attachment plug and a receptacle or cord connector, and individual overload protection is omitted in accordance with 430.42(A), the rating of the attachment plug and receptacle or cord connector shall not exceed 15 amperes at 125 volts or 250 volts. Where individual overload protection is required in accordance with 430.42(B) for a motor or motor-operated appliance that is attached to the branch circuit through an attachment plug and a receptacle or cord connector, the overload device shall be an integral part of the motor or appliance. The rating of the attachment plug and receptacle or cord connector shall determine the rating of the circuit to which the motor can be connected, in accordance with 210.21(B).
records.tip_short: Plug-in motor without its own overload protection: the plug and receptacle are limited to 15 amperes. Correct: A — 15 amps. 430.42(C) limits the plug and receptacle to 15 amperes when individual overload protection is omitted. Not B: 20 amperes exceeds the 15 ampere limit for cord-connected motors without individual overload protection. Not C: 25 amperes is not a standard receptacle rating and exceeds the 15 ampere limit. Not D: 30 amperes is double the 15 ampere maximum set by 430.42(C).
choice_notes: 430.42(C) limits the plug and receptacle to 15 amperes when individual overload protection is omitted.
20 amperes exceeds the 15 ampere limit for cord-connected motors without individual overload protection.
25 amperes is not a standard receptacle rating and exceeds the 15 ampere limit.
30 amperes is double the 15 ampere maximum set by 430.42(C).

records.prompt: ___ is permitted in the dedicated electrical space above a panelboard.
records.gist: The dedicated space above electrical equipment must remain clear of foreign systems. The question asks which one may share that space.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.26(E)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

In plain terms, the question is: "___ is permitted in the dedicated electrical space above a panelboard." Subject: panelboard. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
110.26(E)(1) Indoor
Indoor installations shall comply with 110.26(E)(1)(a) through (E)(1)(d).
(a) Dedicated Electrical Space. The space equal to the width and depth of the equipment and extending from the floor to a height of 1.8 m (6 ft) above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower, shall be dedicated to the electrical installation. No piping, ducts, leak protection apparatus, or other equipment foreign to the electrical installation shall be located in this zone.
Exception: Suspended ceilings with removable panels shall be permitted within the 1.8 m (6 ft) zone.
(b) Foreign Systems. The area above the dedicated space required by 110.26(E)(1)(a) shall be permitted to contain foreign systems, provided protection is installed to avoid damage to the electrical equipment from condensation, leaks, or breaks in such foreign systems.
(c) Sprinkler Protection. Sprinkler protection shall be permitted for the dedicated space where the piping complies with this section.
(d) Suspended Ceilings. A dropped, suspended, or similar ceiling that does not add strength to the building structure shall not be considered a structural ceiling.
records.tip_short: Sprinkler piping is the one foreign system allowed in the dedicated space above a panel, if it complies. Correct: C — Sprinkler protection. 110.26(E)(1) says sprinkler protection shall be permitted for the dedicated space if the piping complies. Not A: Water piping is foreign to the electrical installation and is prohibited in the dedicated space. Not B: Leak protection apparatus is excluded from the dedicated space, though it may be required above it. Not D: Air-conditioning ducts are foreign systems that are not permitted in the dedicated electrical space.
choice_notes: Water piping is foreign to the electrical installation and is prohibited in the dedicated space.
Leak protection apparatus is excluded from the dedicated space, though it may be required above it.
110.26(E)(1) says sprinkler protection shall be permitted for the dedicated space if the piping complies.
Air-conditioning ducts are foreign systems that are not permitted in the dedicated electrical space.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
'Listed' means an independent lab tested it for one specific purpose — use it only that way and follow its instructions, because the instructions are part of the listing. Novelty and special equipment (USB cover plates with night lights, holiday lighting) must be listed, and required markings must be durable and visible where the inspector and the user will actually see them.

Each transformer shall be provided with a nameplate giving the following information:
Name of manufacturer
Rated kilovolt-amperes
Frequency
Primary and secondary voltage
Impedance of transformers 25 kVA and larger
Required clearances for transformers with ventilating openings
Amount and kind of insulating liquid where used
For dry-type transformers, temperature class for the insulation system

Not B: The amount and kind of insulating liquid, where used, is a required 450.11(A) nameplate item. Not D: Required clearances for transformers with ventilating openings must be on the nameplate per 450.11(A).

records.prompt: Branch circuits shall be rated in accordance with the ___.
answers: ampere rating of the largest receptacle
maximum permitted rating of the fuse or breaker
number of receptacle outlets in the branch circuit
ampere rating of the largest conductor
records.gist: A branch circuit's rating is determined by a single element — not its conductors or outlets. The question asks what gives the circuit its rating.
records.article_title: Branch Circuits Not Over 1000 Volts AC, 1500 Volts DC, Nominal
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: switch ampere rating, branch circuit, receptacle outlet. Start with 210.18, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Branch circuits are rated by their breaker: the standard sizes are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amps. A multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit must open all its ungrounded legs together so no leg can stay live alone. And the number of circuits in a building comes from the total load divided by circuit size — fractional results always round up, because half a circuit doesn't exist.

In plain terms, the question is: "Branch circuits shall be rated in accordance with the ___." Subject: branch circuit. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
switch ampere rating, branch circuit, receptacle outlet
records.reference_text:
210.18 Rating
Branch circuits recognized by this article shall be rated in accordance with the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device. The rating for other than individual branch circuits shall be 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes. Where conductors of higher ampacity are used for any reason, the ampere rating or setting of the specified overcurrent device shall determine the circuit rating.
Exception No. 1: Multioutlet branch circuits greater than 50 amperes shall be permitted to supply nonlighting outlet loads in locations where conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the equipment.
Exception No. 2: Branch circuits rated 10 amperes shall not supply receptacle outlets.
records.tip_short: A branch circuit is rated by its breaker or fuse, even when larger wire is used. Correct: B — maximum permitted rating of the fuse or breaker. 210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device. Not A: Receptacle rating does not set the circuit rating; 210.18 uses the overcurrent device rating. Not C: The number of outlets does not determine the rating; the overcurrent device does per 210.18. Not D: 210.18 says larger conductors do not raise the rating; the overcurrent device setting determines it.
choice_notes: Receptacle rating does not set the circuit rating; 210.18 uses the overcurrent device rating.
210.18 rates branch circuits by the maximum permitted ampere rating or setting of the overcurrent device.
The number of outlets does not determine the rating; the overcurrent device does per 210.18.
210.18 says larger conductors do not raise the rating; the overcurrent device setting determines it.

records.prompt: Underground wiring within ___ horizontally from the inside wall of the pool shall be permitted in liquidtight flexible metal conduit listed for direct burial use.
records.gist: Underground wiring near a pool must maintain horizontal separation so fault current cannot reach the water. The question asks how far out that zone goes.
records.article_title: Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit, pool / spa. Start with 680.11(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Water plus electricity is why pools get the strictest rules in the book. Everything metal near the water — shell, ladder, pump, conduit — gets bonded together into one equal-voltage grid so no stray voltage can exist between touchable parts. Receptacles, lights, and fans near the water need GFCI protection, and fixtures above the water must stay high (about 7-1/2 ft with GFCI, 12 ft without) so nobody can touch them from the water.

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Subject: pool. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
conduit, pool / spa
records.reference_text:
680.11(A) Underground Wiring
Underground wiring within 1.5 m (5 ft) horizontally from the inside wall of the pool shall be permitted. The following wiring methods shall be considered suitable for the conditions in these locations provided they are installed complete between outlets, junctions, or splicing points:
Rigid metal conduit
Intermediate metal conduit
Rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit
Reinforced thermosetting resin conduit
Jacketed Type MC cable that is listed for burial use
Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit listed for direct burial use
Liquidtight flexible metal conduit listed for direct burial use

Not A: 18 inches is not the distance; 680.11(A) covers wiring within 1.5 m (5 feet), which is 60 inches. Not B: 24 inches is too short; the 680.11(A) zone is 5 feet, or 60 inches. Not C: 48 inches is only 4 feet; 680.11(A) uses 1.5 m (5 feet), which is 60 inches.

records.prompt: You have 125 volts at the panel and 115 volts at the load. What is the percentage of voltage drop?
records.gist: A 10-volt difference exists between the panel and the load. The question asks what share of the starting 125 volts that loss is. Divide volts lost by source volts.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: voltage drop, load calculation. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This asks what percentage of voltage is lost between source and load. Numbers in the question: 125 volts, 115 volts. Divide the volts lost by the source volts.

LOOKUP FOCUS
voltage drop, load calculation
records.reference_text:
Voltage Drop Calculation
VD = V_source - V_load = 125V - 115V = 10V drop.
% Voltage Drop = (10V / 125V) * 100 = 8%.
records.tip_short: Percent voltage drop is volts lost divided by source volts: 10 volts out of 125 is 8 percent. Correct: D — 8%. The drop is 125 minus 115, or 10 volts, and 10 divided by 125 is 8 percent. Not A: 5 percent would be a 6.25 volt drop; the actual drop is 10 volts, or 8 percent. Not B: 4.35 percent is 5 divided by 115, using the wrong drop and the wrong base voltage. Not C: 4.17 percent is 5 divided by 120, not the 10 volt drop over 125 volts.
records.formula: % Drop = ((V_panel - V_load) / V_panel) × 100
choice_notes: 5 percent would be a 6.25 volt drop; the actual drop is 10 volts, or 8 percent.
4.35 percent is 5 divided by 115, using the wrong drop and the wrong base voltage.
4.17 percent is 5 divided by 120, not the 10 volt drop over 125 volts.
The drop is 125 minus 115, or 10 volts, and 10 divided by 125 is 8 percent.

records.prompt: 60 cycle frequency travels 90 degrees in how many seconds?
records.gist: Alternating current reverses 60 times per second; the question covers one quarter-cycle. Compute the duration of one quarter-cycle.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

In plain terms, the question is: "60 cycle frequency travels 90 degrees in how many seconds?" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
AC Waveform Period and Phase Angle
One full cycle = 360 degrees = 1/60 second = 0.01667 s.
90 degrees is 1/4 of a cycle: (1/60) / 4 = 1/240 second (0.00417 s).
records.tip_short: At 60 hertz one full 360 degree cycle takes 1/60 second, so 90 degrees is a quarter of that: 1/240 second. Correct: D — 1/240. 90 degrees is one quarter of a cycle, and 1/60 divided by 4 is 1/240 second. Not A: 1/60 second is a full 360 degree cycle, not 90 degrees. Not B: 1/120 second is a half cycle, or 180 degrees. Not C: 1/180 second is one-third of a cycle, or 120 degrees.
records.formula: t = (Angle / 360) × (1 / Frequency)
records.worked: One cycle (360°) at 60 Hz takes 1/60 sec. 90° is 1/4 cycle: (1/60) * (1/4) = 1/240 second.
choice_notes: 1/60 second is a full 360 degree cycle, not 90 degrees.
1/120 second is a half cycle, or 180 degrees.
1/180 second is one-third of a cycle, or 120 degrees.
90 degrees is one quarter of a cycle, and 1/60 divided by 4 is 1/240 second.

records.prompt: Type MC cable shall be permitted to be unsupported and unsecured where the cable is not more than ___ in length from the last point of connection to luminaires.
records.gist: A short length of flexible raceway serving a luminaire is exempt from standard support intervals. The question asks how long that free length may be.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: MI = Mineral-Insulated (wires in white mineral powder inside a copper tube — fireproof, for hazardous and harsh spots). MC = Metal-Clad (metal armor, goes almost anywhere). NM = Nonmetallic-sheathed, Romex (dry homes only). UF = Underground Feeder (burial and wet spots). SE = Service-Entrance (brings power in). AC = Armored Cable/BX (grounds through its armor plus a bonding strip, needs a red anti-short bushing). USE stays buried outside and may not come indoors.

cable

330.30(D) Unsupported Cables

Is fished between access points through concealed spaces in finished buildings or structures and supporting is impractical
Is not more than 1.8 m (6 ft) in length from the last point of cable support to the point of connection to luminaires or other electrical equipment and the cable and point of connection are within an accessible ceiling
Is Type MC of the interlocked armor type in lengths not exceeding 900 mm (3 ft) from the last point where it is securely fastened and is used to connect equipment where flexibility is necessary to minimize the transmission of vibration from equipment or to provide flexibility for equipment that requires movement after installation

Not A: 36 inches is the limit for interlocked MC used for flexibility, not for luminaire connections. Not B: 48 inches is too short; 330.30(D)(2) allows up to 1.8 m (6 feet), which is 72 inches. Not C: 60 inches is too short; the limit is 6 feet, which is 72 inches.

48 inches is too short; 330.30(D)(2) allows up to 1.8 m (6 feet), which is 72 inches.
60 inches is too short; the limit is 6 feet, which is 72 inches.

records.prompt: What is the minimum size equipment grounding conductor for a 50 amp rated branch circuit?
records.gist: The equipment grounding conductor is selected from its table using the upstream overcurrent device rating. A 50-amp breaker is given. The question asks the copper size across from it.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: equipment grounding conductor, branch circuit. Start with Table 250.122, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: branch circuit. Numbers in the question: 50 amp. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
equipment grounding conductor, branch circuit
records.reference_text:

15	14	12
20	12	10
60	10	8
100	8	6

Not A: 14 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 15 ampere device, far too small for 50 amperes. Not B: 12 AWG copper is the grounding conductor for a 20 ampere device, too small for 50 amperes. Not D: 8 AWG copper is the size for devices up to 100 amperes; 10 AWG copper is the minimum at 50 amperes.

records.prompt: What is the full load current of a 50 horsepower, three-phase, 480v, wound-rotor AC motor?
records.gist: Motor current comes from the Code's own table, never the nameplate, and a 480-volt system uses the 460-volt column. The question asks what a 50-horse wound-rotor motor reads there.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, load calculation. Start with Table 430.250, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

This asks you to match this motor or transformer setup to its rule. Subject: motor. Identify whether the question is about protection size, conductor size, disconnect location, or marking.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

records.prompt: The motor branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protective device must be capable of carrying the ___ current of the motor.

records.prompt: Voltage drop on sensitive electronic equipment systems must not exceed ___ for branch circuits.
records.gist: Sensitive electronic equipment on separately derived 120-volt systems has tighter voltage-drop limits than ordinary wiring. The question asks the limit for branch circuits alone.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, voltage drop. Start with 647.4(D), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This asks what percentage of voltage is lost between source and load. Subject: branch circuit. Divide the volts lost by the source volts.

LOOKUP FOCUS
branch circuit, voltage drop
records.reference_text:
647.4(D) Voltage Drop
The voltage drop on any branch circuit shall not exceed 1.5 percent. The combined voltage drop of feeder and branch-circuit conductors shall not exceed 2.5 percent.
(1) Fixed Equipment
The voltage drop on branch circuits supplying equipment connected using wiring methods in Chapter 3 shall not exceed 1.5 percent. The combined voltage drop of feeder and branch-circuit conductors shall not exceed 2.5 percent.
(2) Cord-Connected Equipment
The voltage drop on branch circuits supplying receptacles shall not exceed 1 percent. For the purposes of making this calculation, the load connected to the receptacle outlet shall be considered to be 50 percent of the branch-circuit rating. The combined voltage drop of feeder and branch-circuit conductors shall not exceed 2.0 percent.

Correct: A — 1.5%. 647.4(D) limits branch-circuit voltage drop to 1.5 percent. Not B: 2.5 percent is the combined feeder and branch-circuit limit in 647.4(D), not the branch limit. Not C: 3 percent is the general informational note value for branch circuits, not the 647.4(D) limit. Not D: 5 percent is the general combined recommendation, far above the 647.4(D) limit of 1.5 percent.

5 percent is the general combined recommendation, far above the 647.4(D) limit of 1.5 percent.

records.prompt: The definition of “fibers/flyings, ignitible” is found in Article ___.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Hazardous locations are sorted by what's in the air. Class I means flammable gases or vapors (gasoline, spray booths). Class II means combustible dust (grain, flour, coal). Class III means ignitable fibers or flyings (textiles, wood shops, cotton). Division 1 means the hazard is there during normal work; Division 2 means only if something goes wrong. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. records.prompt: Refer to the figure below. GIVEN: Switch S1 is in the "ON" position, but the light does not come on. Voltage across L1 is measured to be 120 volts. Voltage across S1 is measured to be 0 volts. The light does not come on because ___.

there is a break in the wiring of the circuit

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A switch is rated for what it interrupts. Ordinary snap switches handle lighting loads, but inductive loads like motors and ballasts punish contacts, so the NEC caps them at half the switch's ampere rating. A three-way switch is secretly a single-pole double-throw — one lever flipping power between two traveler paths, which is why two of them team up to control one light from two places.

Not B: A short would read near 0 volts across the shorted part and likely trip the breaker, not show 120 volts. Not C: A switch that failed to make contact would show 120 volts across the switch, not 0 volts. Not D: A wiring break would put the voltage across the break, so the lamp would read 0 volts.

Where there is no objection because of weakening the building structure, in both exposed and concealed locations, cables or raceways shall be permitted to be laid in notches in wood studs, joists, rafters, or other wood members where the cable or raceway at those points is protected from penetration by nails or screws by a steel plate at least 1.6 mm (1/16 in.) thick, and of appropriate length and width, installed to cover the area of the wiring. The steel plate shall be installed before the building finish is applied.
Exception No. 1: Steel plates shall not be required to protect rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, rigid nonmetallic conduit, or electrical metallic tubing.
Exception No. 2: A listed and marked steel plate less than 1.6 mm (1/16 in.) thick that provides equal or better protection against nail or screw penetration shall be permitted.
records.tip_short: Nail plates over notched studs must be at least 1/16 inch steel, unless a listed thinner plate gives equal protection. Correct: A — 1/16". 300.4(A)(2) requires a steel plate at least 1.6 mm (1/16 inch) thick over the notch. Not B: 3/32 inch is thicker than required; the Code minimum is 1/16 inch. Not C: 1/8 inch exceeds the minimum; 300.4(A)(2) requires only 1/16 inch steel plate. Not D: 3/16 inch is three times the required 1/16 inch minimum thickness.
choice_notes: 300.4(A)(2) requires a steel plate at least 1.6 mm (1/16 inch) thick over the notch.
3/32 inch is thicker than required; the Code minimum is 1/16 inch.
1/8 inch exceeds the minimum; 300.4(A)(2) requires only 1/16 inch steel plate.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

This asks where GFCI protection is required. Subject: receptacle. Numbers in the question: 20 amp. Match the location and equipment in the question to the list of places the NEC names.

records.reference_text:
210.63 Equipment Requiring Servicing
A 125-volt, single-phase, 15- or 20-ampere-rated receptacle outlet shall be installed at an accessible location within 7.5 m (25 ft) of the equipment as specified in 210.63(A) and (B).
Informational Note: See 210.8(E) for requirements on GFCI protection.
(A) Heating, Air-Conditioning, and Refrigeration Equipment
The required receptacle outlet shall be located on the same level as the heating, air-conditioning, and refrigeration equipment. The receptacle outlet shall not be connected to the load side of the equipment's branch-circuit disconnecting means.
Exception: A receptacle outlet shall not be required at one- and two-family dwellings for the service of evaporative coolers.
(B) Other Electrical Equipment
In other than one- and two-family dwellings, a receptacle outlet shall be located as specified in 210.63(B)(1) and (B)(2).
(1) Indoor Service Equipment
The required receptacle outlet shall be located within the same room or area as the service equipment.
(2) Indoor Equipment Requiring Dedicated Equipment Spaces
Where equipment, other than service equipment, requires dedicated equipment space as specified in 110.26(E), the required receptacle outlet shall be located within the same room or area as the electrical equipment and shall not be connected to the load side of the equipment's disconnecting means.
records.tip_short: Equipment needing service gets a 125-volt receptacle within 25 feet, and 210.8(E) makes that receptacle GFCI protected. Correct: A — 25. 210.63 requires the receptacle outlet within 7.5 m (25 ft) of the equipment. Not B: 30 feet exceeds the 210.63 limit of 25 feet. Not C: 45 feet is well beyond the 25 feet required by 210.63. Not D: 50 feet is double the 25-foot maximum in 210.63.

records.prompt: Alternating current snap switches shall be permitted for control of inductive loads not exceeding ___ of the ampere rating of the switch at the applied voltage.
records.gist: A snap switch interrupting motor or ballast loads is subject to arcing and is limited below its lamp rating. The question asks what share of its rating it may switch.
keywords: rating and use of snap switches
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: rating and use of snap switches, inductive loads, applied voltage, switch ampere rating. Start with 404.14(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A switch is rated for what it interrupts. Ordinary snap switches handle lighting loads, but inductive loads like motors and ballasts punish contacts, so the NEC caps them at half the switch's ampere rating. A three-way switch is secretly a single-pole double-throw — one lever flipping power between two traveler paths, which is why two of them team up to control one light from two places.

This asks which switch rule fits. Check whether the question is about the ampere rating, the type of load, or where and how the switch is installed.

records.reference_text:
404.14(B) Alternating-Current or Direct-Current General-Use Snap Switch
This form of switch shall be permitted on either ac or dc circuits and used only for controlling the following:
(1) Resistive loads not exceeding the ampere rating of the switch at the voltage applied.
(2) Inductive loads not exceeding 50 percent of the ampere rating of the switch at the applied voltage. Switches rated in horsepower are suitable for controlling motor loads within their rating at the voltage applied.
(3) Tungsten-filament lamp loads not exceeding the ampere rating of the switch at the applied voltage if T-rated.
(4) Electronic ballasts, self-ballasted lamps, compact fluorescent lamps, and LED lamp loads with their associated drivers, not exceeding the ampere rating of the switch at the voltage applied.
records.tip_short: General-use snap switches handle inductive loads only up to 50 percent of their ampere rating, unless horsepower rated. Correct: C — 50%. 404.14(B) permits inductive loads not exceeding 50 percent of the switch ampere rating. Not A: 70 percent is not in 404.14(B); inductive loads are limited to 50 percent of the switch rating. Not B: 60 percent is too high; 404.14(B) caps inductive loads at 50 percent of the ampere rating. Not D: 33 percent is more restrictive than the Code; the limit is 50 percent.
choice_notes: 70 percent is not in 404.14(B); inductive loads are limited to 50 percent of the switch rating.
60 percent is too high; 404.14(B) caps inductive loads at 50 percent of the ampere rating.
404.14(B) permits inductive loads not exceeding 50 percent of the switch ampere rating.

records.prompt: Other than the required interconnections and control wiring, only those conductors that are intended for termination in a/an ___ section of a switchboard or switchgear shall be located in that section.
records.gist: Conductors passing through sections they do not terminate in create hazards. Only conductors terminating in a section may occupy it. The question asks which kind of section a wire must end in to sit there.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conductors. Start with 408.3(A)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

This asks which switch rule fits. Subject: switchboard. Check whether the question is about the ampere rating, the type of load, or where and how the switch is installed.

records.reference_text:
408.3(A)(2) Same Vertical Section
Other than the required interconnections and control wiring, only those conductors that are intended for termination in a vertical section of a switchboard or switchgear shall be located in that section.
Exception: Conductors shall be permitted to travel horizontally through vertical sections of switchboards and switchgear where such conductors are isolated from busbars by a barrier.
records.tip_short: Each vertical section of switchgear carries only its own conductors; pass-through wiring needs a barrier from busbars. Correct: C — vertical. 408.3(A)(2) limits conductors in a vertical section to those terminating in that section. Not A: Isolated is not the term used; 408.3(A)(2) refers to a vertical section. Not B: Horizontal travel is only an exception when barriered; the rule applies to each vertical section. Not D: Dual section is not an NEC term; 408.3(A)(2) addresses vertical sections.
choice_notes: Isolated is not the term used; 408.3(A)(2) refers to a vertical section.
Horizontal travel is only an exception when barriered; the rule applies to each vertical section.
408.3(A)(2) limits conductors in a vertical section to those terminating in that section.
Dual section is not an NEC term; 408.3(A)(2) addresses vertical sections.

records.prompt: Plate electrodes shall be installed not less than ___ below the surface of earth.
records.gist: A plate electrode is effective only in permanently moist earth at sufficient depth. The question asks how deep it must be buried.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 250.53(A)(5), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This is a minimum-limit question. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
250.53(A)(5) Plate Electrode
Plate electrodes shall be installed not less than 750 mm (30 in.) below the surface of the earth.
records.tip_short: Plate electrodes go 30 inches deep, which is 2 1/2 feet; ground rods need 8 feet in contact with soil. Correct: B — 2 1/2 feet. 250.53(A)(5) requires 750 mm (30 inches), and 30 inches equals 2 1/2 feet. Not A: 2 feet is 24 inches, shallower than the 750 mm (30 inches) required by 250.53(A)(5). Not C: 3 feet is 36 inches, deeper than the 30-inch minimum, so it is not the Code value. Not D: 4 feet is 48 inches, well past the 30-inch minimum, so it is not the Code value.
choice_notes: 2 feet is 24 inches, shallower than the 750 mm (30 inches) required by 250.53(A)(5).
250.53(A)(5) requires 750 mm (30 inches), and 30 inches equals 2 1/2 feet.
3 feet is 36 inches, deeper than the 30-inch minimum, so it is not the Code value.
4 feet is 48 inches, well past the 30-inch minimum, so it is not the Code value.

408.41 Grounded Conductor Terminations
Each grounded conductor shall terminate within the panelboard in an individual terminal that is not also used for another conductor.
Exception: Grounded conductors of circuits with parallel conductors shall be permitted to terminate in a single terminal if the terminal is identified for connection of more than one conductor.

Correct: D — individual. 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in its own individual terminal, not shared with another. Not A: Single is close but not the Code term; 408.41 requires an individual terminal for each grounded conductor. Not B: Multiwire describes a type of branch circuit, not a neutral terminal. Not C: A dual terminal would hold two conductors, which 408.41 prohibits except for parallel conductors.

210.8(A) Dwelling Units
All 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles installed in the following locations and supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground shall have ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel:
(1) Bathrooms

records.prompt: When normally enclosed live parts are exposed for inspection or servicing, the working space, if in a passageway or general open space, shall be suitably ___.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Working space is the empty bubble an electrician stands in while servicing live gear — nobody may store boxes or park equipment in it. The NEC measures it three ways: depth in front (3+ ft depending on voltage and what faces the gear — concrete or brick walls facing you mean deeper space), 30 in. minimum width (or the equipment's width), and 6-1/2 ft of headroom. Big gear needs doors that swing 90° and a way out that open doors can't block. Above panels, the space up to the ceiling belongs to electrics only — no pipes or ducts.
