Working space required by this section shall not be used for storage. When normally enclosed live parts are exposed for inspection or servicing, the working space, if in a passageway or general open space, shall be suitably guarded.

Not A: Isolated is not the term; 110.26(B) requires the working space to be suitably guarded. Not B: Locking is not required by 110.26(B); the space must be suitably guarded. Not D: Insulating the space is not the requirement; 110.26(B) calls for it to be guarded.

records.prompt: As it relates to load calculations, calculations shall be permitted to be rounded to the nearest whole ampere, with decimal fractions smaller than ___ dropped.
records.gist: Load calculations do not require extended decimal precision. The question asks how small a fraction you may simply drop.
records.article_title: Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: load calculation. Start with 220.5(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This is a load-calculation question. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

LOOKUP FOCUS
load calculation
records.reference_text:
220.5(B) Fractions of an Ampere
Calculations shall be permitted to be rounded to the nearest whole ampere, with decimal fractions smaller than 0.5 dropped.
records.tip_short: Load calculation rounding: 0.5 and above rounds up to the next ampere; anything below 0.5 is dropped. Correct: A — 0.5. 220.5(B) permits rounding to the nearest whole ampere, dropping decimal fractions smaller than 0.5. Not B: 0.05 is not the threshold; 220.5(B) drops fractions smaller than 0.5. Not C: 0.6 would not be normal rounding; the Code uses 0.5 as the cutoff. Not D: 0.8 is a common continuous-load factor, not the 220.5(B) rounding threshold.
choice_notes: 220.5(B) permits rounding to the nearest whole ampere, dropping decimal fractions smaller than 0.5.

0.6 would not be normal rounding; the Code uses 0.5 as the cutoff.
0.8 is a common continuous-load factor, not the 220.5(B) rounding threshold.

408.18(C) Connections
Each section of equipment that requires rear or side access to make field connections shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the front. Section openings requiring rear or side access shall comply with 110.26. Load terminals for field wiring shall comply with 408.18(C)(1), (C)(2), or (C)(3) as applicable.

Load terminals for field wiring shall be so located that it is not necessary to reach across uninsulated ungrounded bus in order to make connections.
(2) Grounded Circuit Conductors
Where multiple branch or feeder grounded circuit conductor load terminals for field wiring are grouped together in one location, they shall be so located that it is not necessary to reach across uninsulated ungrounded bus, whether or not energized, in order to make connections.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: load calculation. Start with Table 220.42(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This is a load-calculation question. Numbers in the question: 5,000 sq. ft. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A disconnecting means is simply the switch or breaker a worker opens before touching equipment. The golden rule is 'within sight': visible and no more than 50 ft away, so nobody can re-energize it unseen. Motors need a disconnect in sight of both the controller and the motor itself; appliances and AC units need one in sight and quickly reachable. If the disconnect must live far away, it has to be lockable open with the location marked on the equipment.

A box, conduit body, or other enclosure, with a cover installed, shall be required for all splices.
Exception No. 1: On construction sites, a box, conduit body, or other enclosure shall not be required for either of the following conditions:
(1) The circuit conductors being spliced are all from nonmetallic multiconductor cord or cable assemblies, provided that the equipment grounding continuity is maintained with or without the box.
(2) The circuit conductors being spliced, are all from metal-sheathed cable assemblies terminated in listed fittings that mechanically secure the cable sheath to maintain effective electrical continuity.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: dwelling unit. Start with Table 220.54, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

In plain terms, the question is: "The permitted demand factor for five household clothes dryers in a multifamily dwelling is ___." Subject: dwelling unit. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
dwelling unit
records.reference_text:
Table 220.54 Demand Factors for Household Electric Clothes Dryers
Number of Dryers	Demand Factor (%)
1–4	100%
5	85%
6	75%
7	65%
8	60%
9	55%
10	50%
11	47%
12–23	47% minus 1% for each dryer exceeding 11
24–42	35% minus 0.5% for each dryer exceeding 23
43 and over	25%
reference_table: NOTE: Each dryer counts at 5000 watts (volt-amperes) or its nameplate rating, whichever is larger (220.54).
records.tip_short: Dryer demand in Table 220.54: 1 to 4 dryers are 100 percent, 5 are 85, 6 are 75, 7 are 65, 8 are 60. Correct: D — 85%. Table 220.54 assigns an 85 percent demand factor to five household clothes dryers. Not A: 70 percent is not a Table 220.54 value for any dryer count from 5 to 11; 6 dryers are 75 percent and 7 are 65 percent. Not B: 75 percent is the Table 220.54 demand factor for 6 dryers, not 5. Not C: 80 percent is not a Table 220.54 value; the factor drops from 85 percent at 5 dryers to 75 percent at 6.
records.formula: Multiple dryers use the Table 220.54 demand factor for that dryer count.
choice_notes: 70 percent is not a Table 220.54 value for any dryer count from 5 to 11; 6 dryers are 75 percent and 7 are 65 percent.
75 percent is the Table 220.54 demand factor for 6 dryers, not 5.
80 percent is not a Table 220.54 value; the factor drops from 85 percent at 5 dryers to 75 percent at 6.
Table 220.54 assigns an 85 percent demand factor to five household clothes dryers.

records.prompt: A controller that includes motor overload protection ___ for group motor application shall be marked with the motor overload protection and the maximum branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for such applications.
records.gist: A controller serving a motor group must display a marking identifying its protection. The question asks which word the Code requires in that marking.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground fault, motor, load calculation. Start with 430.8, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: motor. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS

records.reference_text:
430.8 Marking on Motor Controllers
A motor controller that includes motor overload protection suitable for group motor application shall be marked with the motor overload protection and the maximum branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for such applications.
Combination motor controllers that employ adjustable instantaneous trip circuit breakers shall be clearly marked to indicate the ampere settings of the adjustable trip element.
records.tip_short: A controller whose overload protection is suitable for group motor use must be marked with its overload and max SCPD rating. Correct: D — suitable. 430.8 covers controllers with motor overload protection suitable for group motor application. Not A: 430.8 does not say required; it describes overload protection suitable for group motor application. Not B: Recognized is not the word used; 430.8 says suitable for group motor application. Not C: Permitted is not the word used; 430.8 says suitable for group motor application.

Recognized is not the word used; 430.8 says suitable for group motor application.
Permitted is not the word used; 430.8 says suitable for group motor application.

records.prompt: Type UF cable is permitted to be used ___.
answers: for wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations
records.gist: Type UF cable is rated for wet, dry, and corrosive soil. The question asks where it may run, and three answers are places it forbids.
records.article_title: Underground Feeder and Branch-Circuit Cable: Type UF
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable. Start with 340.10(3), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: MI = Mineral-Insulated (wires in white mineral powder inside a copper tube — fireproof, for hazardous and harsh spots). MC = Metal-Clad (metal armor, goes almost anywhere). NM = Nonmetallic-sheathed, Romex (dry homes only). UF = Underground Feeder (burial and wet spots). SE = Service-Entrance (brings power in). AC = Armored Cable/BX (grounds through its armor plus a bonding strip, needs a red anti-short bushing). USE stays buried outside and may not come indoors.

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Subject: Type UF cable. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
cable
records.reference_text:
340.10 Uses Permitted
Type UF cable shall be permitted as follows:
(1) For use underground, including direct burial in the earth.
(2) As single-conductor cables. Where installed as single-conductor cables, all conductors of the feeder or branch circuit, including the grounded conductor and equipment grounding conductor, if any, shall be installed in accordance with 300.3.
(3) For wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations.
(4) Installed as nonmetallic-sheathed cable. Where so installed, the installation and conductor requirements shall comply with Parts II and III of Article 334, except for 334.12(B), and shall be of the multiconductor type.
(5) As single-conductor cables as the nonheating leads for heating cables as provided in 424.43.
(6) Supported by cable trays. Type UF cable supported by cable trays shall be of the multiconductor type.
Informational Note: See 310.14(A)(3) for temperature limitation of conductors.
records.tip_short: UF means Underground Feeder: 340.10 allows it in wet, dry, or corrosive locations, and for direct burial. Correct: D — for wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations. 340.10 permits Type UF cable for wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations. Not A: 340.12 prohibits Type UF cable as service-entrance cable. Not B: 340.12 prohibits Type UF cable in commercial garages. Not C: 340.12 prohibits Type UF cable where subject to physical damage.
choice_notes: 340.12 prohibits Type UF cable as service-entrance cable.
340.12 prohibits Type UF cable in commercial garages.

340.10 permits Type UF cable for wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations.

records.prompt: Cables with entirely nonmetallic sheaths shall be permitted to enter the top of a surface-mounted enclosure through one or more nonflexible raceways not less than ___ and not more than 10 feet in length, provided all conditions are met.
records.gist: Type NM cable may enter surface enclosures through short lengths of protective raceway. The question asks the shortest those sleeves may be.
records.article_title: Cabinets, Cutout Boxes, and Meter Socket Enclosures
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: raceway, cable. Start with 312.5(C) Ex. 1, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: raceway. Numbers in the question: 10 feet. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
raceway, cable
records.reference_text:
312.5(C) Cables
Where cable is used, each cable shall be secured to the cabinet, cutout box, or meter socket enclosure.
Exception No. 1: Cables with entirely nonmetallic sheaths shall be permitted to enter the top of a surface-mounted enclosure through one or more nonflexible raceways not less than 450 mm (18 in.) and not more than 3.0 m (10 ft) in length, provided all of the following conditions are met:
(1) Each cable is fastened within 300 mm (12 in.), measured along the sheath, of the outer end of the raceway.
(2) The raceway extends directly above the enclosure and does not penetrate a structural ceiling.
(3) A fitting is provided on each end of the raceway to protect the cable(s) from abrasion and the fittings remain accessible after installation.
(4) The raceway is sealed or plugged at the outer end using approved means so as to prevent access to the enclosure through the raceway.
(5) The cable sheath is continuous through the raceway and extends into the enclosure beyond the fitting not less than 6 mm (1/4 in.).
(6) The raceway is fastened at its outer end and at other points in accordance with the applicable article.
(7) Where installed as conduit or tubing, the cable fill does not exceed the amount that would be permitted for complete conduit or tubing systems by Table 1 of Chapter 9 of this Code and all applicable notes thereto.
records.tip_short: Nonmetallic cable sleeve into a panel top: raceway 18 inches minimum to 10 feet maximum, cable fastened within 12 inches. Correct: C — 18 inches. 312.5(C) Exception No. 1 requires the raceway to be not less than 450 mm (18 inches) long. Not A: 12 inches is the fastening distance from the raceway end, not the minimum raceway length. Not B: 16 inches is not a value in 312.5(C) Exception No. 1. Not D: 24 inches exceeds the minimum; the Code minimum raceway length is 18 inches.
choice_notes: 12 inches is the fastening distance from the raceway end, not the minimum raceway length.
16 inches is not a value in 312.5(C) Exception No. 1.
312.5(C) Exception No. 1 requires the raceway to be not less than 450 mm (18 inches) long.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground-fault circuit-interrupter, branch circuit, receptacle outlet, dwelling unit. Start with 210.8(A) Ex. 1, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

This asks where GFCI protection is required. Subject: receptacle. Match the location and equipment in the question to the list of places the NEC names.

LOOKUP FOCUS

All 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles installed in the following locations and supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground shall have ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel:

Exception No. 1: Receptacles that are not readily accessible and are supplied by a branch circuit dedicated to electric snow-melting, deicing, or pipeline and vessel heating equipment shall be permitted to be installed in accordance with 426.28 or 427.22, as applicable.

Not C: Covered is not the condition in 210.8(A) Exception No. 1.

records.prompt: For a service rated 100 through 400 amps, the service conductors supplying the entire load of a one-family dwelling shall be permitted to have an ampacity of ___ of the service rating.
records.gist: A dwelling service is not fully loaded, so its conductors may be sized below the service rating. The question asks what share of the rating they may be.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, conductors, dwelling unit, load calculation. Start with 310.12(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Services and transformers are about size and labels. A one-family dwelling service from 100–400 A may use conductors at 83% of the rating (the diversity of a home makes full size unnecessary). Every transformer must wear a nameplate with its ratings — but not trivia like the wire gauge inside it. And transformers generally need a disconnect in sight, or lockable with its location marked on the unit.

This asks how many amps the conductor may safely carry under the stated conditions. Subject: dwelling unit. Numbers in the question: 400 amps. Apply temperature and adjustment factors first, then read the resulting ampacity.

LOOKUP FOCUS
ampacity, conductors, dwelling unit, load calculation
records.reference_text:
310.12(A) Services
For a service rated 100 amperes through 400 amperes, the service conductors supplying the entire load associated with a one-family dwelling, or the service conductors supplying the entire load associated with an individual dwelling unit in a two-family or multifamily dwelling, shall be permitted to have an ampacity not less than 83 percent of the service rating.
records.tip_short: Dwelling services from 100 to 400 amperes may use conductors rated 83 percent of the service rating, per 310.12(A). Correct: A — 83%. 310.12(A) permits an ampacity not less than 83 percent of the service rating for 100 to 400 amperes. Not B: 80 percent is a common continuous-load figure, not the 310.12(A) dwelling service value. Not C: 75 percent is not the value in 310.12(A); the Code uses 83 percent. Not D: 70 percent is not the value in 310.12(A); the Code uses 83 percent.

records.prompt: One or more metal in-ground support structures in direct contact with the earth vertically for ___ feet or more, with or without concrete encasement, is a permitted grounding electrode.
records.gist: A structural steel column may serve as an electrode only with sufficient earth contact. The question asks how many feet must be buried.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounding electrode. Start with 250.52(A)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This asks you to name the grounding or bonding part in this installation. Subject: grounding electrode. Trace the fault-current path: what connects the equipment back to the source?

LOOKUP FOCUS
grounding electrode
records.reference_text:
250.52(A)(2) Metal In-Ground Support Structure(s)
One or more metal in-ground support structure(s) in direct contact with the earth vertically for 3.0 m (10 ft) or more, with or without concrete encasement. If multiple metal in-ground support structures are present at a building or a structure, it shall be permissible to bond only one into the grounding electrode system.
Informational Note: Metal in-ground support structures include, but are not limited to, pilings, casings, and other structural metal.
records.tip_short: Metal pilings or casings count as a grounding electrode if at least 10 feet are in direct contact with earth. Correct: C — 10. 250.52(A)(2) requires direct earth contact vertically for 3.0 m (10 feet) or more. Not A: 6 feet is too short; 250.52(A)(2) requires 3.0 m (10 feet) or more in earth contact. Not B: 8 feet is the ground rod length, not the in-ground support structure length. Not D: 12 feet exceeds the minimum; the Code requires 10 feet or more.
choice_notes: 6 feet is too short; 250.52(A)(2) requires 3.0 m (10 feet) or more in earth contact.
8 feet is the ground rod length, not the in-ground support structure length.
250.52(A)(2) requires direct earth contact vertically for 3.0 m (10 feet) or more.
12 feet exceeds the minimum; the Code requires 10 feet or more.

records.prompt: Which of the following cord types is permitted in a wet location and is sunlight resistant?
records.gist: Outdoor flexible cords require weather-resistant construction identified by their type letters. The question asks which of these four types is rated for wet and sunny.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with Table 400.4 and Note 9, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

Read the situation, then test each choice against it. Eliminate choices that contradict the stated conditions; the survivor that fits all of them is the answer.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Table 400.4 Flexible Cords and Flexible Cables
Cords that comply with the requirements for outdoor cords and are so listed shall be permitted to be designated as weather and water resistant with the suffix "W" after the Code type designation. Cords with the "W" suffix are suitable for use in wet locations and are sunlight resistant.
reference_table: NOTE: Table 400.4 Note 9: cords with the "W" suffix are suitable for use in wet locations and are sunlight resistant.
records.tip_short: In cord codes, W means wet-location and sunlight-resistant, so STOOW is the outdoor-rated flexible cord. Correct: B — STOOW. Table 400.4 lists STOOW as permitted in wet locations and sunlight resistant; the W suffix shows this. Not A: SPT-2 is parallel thermoplastic lamp cord and is not marked for wet locations or sunlight resistance. Not C: THWN is a building wire in Table 310.4(1), not a flexible cord type in Table 400.4. Not D: XHWN is a building wire in Table 310.4(1), not a flexible cord type in Table 400.4.
choice_notes: SPT-2 is parallel thermoplastic lamp cord and is not marked for wet locations or sunlight resistance.
Table 400.4 lists STOOW as permitted in wet locations and sunlight resistant; the W suffix shows this.
THWN is a building wire in Table 310.4(1), not a flexible cord type in Table 400.4.
XHWN is a building wire in Table 310.4(1), not a flexible cord type in Table 400.4.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). records.gist: The 2023 Code dropped one item from the list of spaces left out of dwelling floor area. The question asks which space is now counted.
records.article_title: Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: dwelling unit, floor area, load calculation. Start with 220.5(C), then compare its exclusion list with each choice.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This is a load-calculation question. Subject: dwelling unit. Find the unit load for the occupancy, multiply by the area or quantity, and apply any demand factor the question allows.

LOOKUP FOCUS
dwelling unit, load calculation
records.reference_text:
220.5(C) Floor Area
The floor area for each floor shall be calculated from the outside dimensions of the building, dwelling unit, or other area involved. For dwelling units, the calculated floor area shall not include open porches or unfinished areas not adaptable for future use as a habitable room or occupiable space.
records.tip_short: 2023 floor area excludes only open porches and unfinished unadaptable areas, so garages now count. Correct: B — garages. 220.5(C) no longer excludes garages, so garage area is included. Not A: 220.5(C) says dwelling floor area shall not include open porches. Not C: 220.5(C) excludes unfinished areas not adaptable for future habitable or occupiable use. Not D: All of these fails because open porches and unadaptable areas are excluded.
choice_notes: 220.5(C) says dwelling floor area shall not include open porches.
220.5(C) no longer excludes garages, so garage area is included.
220.5(C) excludes unfinished areas not adaptable for future habitable or occupiable use.

records.prompt: Where overcurrent protection is provided as part of the industrial control panel, the supply conductors shall be considered as either feeders or ___ as covered by 240.21.
records.gist: Conductors leaving an industrial panel fall into two classifications, each with its own rules. The question asks which one these supply wires count as.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, feeder, overcurrent protection, conductors. Start with 409.21(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

In plain terms, the question is: "Where overcurrent protection is provided as part of the industrial control panel, the supply conductors shall be considered as either…" Subject: feeder. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
branch circuit, feeder, overcurrent protection, conductors
records.reference_text:
409.21 Overcurrent Protection
(A) General
Industrial control panels shall be provided with overcurrent protection in accordance with Parts I and II of Article 240.
(B) Location
This protection shall be provided for each incoming supply circuit by either of the following:
(1) An overcurrent protective device located ahead of the industrial control panel.
(2) A single main overcurrent protective device located within the industrial control panel. Where overcurrent protection is provided as part of the industrial control panel, the supply conductors shall be considered as either feeders or taps as covered by 240.21.
records.tip_short: With the main OCPD inside the control panel, its supply conductors are treated as feeders or taps under 240.21. Correct: A — taps. 409.21(B) says the supply conductors are considered either feeders or taps as covered by 240.21. Not B: Branch circuits are not an option named in 409.21(B); it says feeders or taps. Not C: Shunts are not a conductor classification in 409.21(B). Not D: Isolated is not a conductor classification in 409.21(B).
choice_notes: 409.21(B) says the supply conductors are considered either feeders or taps as covered by 240.21.
Branch circuits are not an option named in 409.21(B); it says feeders or taps.
Shunts are not a conductor classification in 409.21(B).
Isolated is not a conductor classification in 409.21(B).

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

records.prompt: ___. An electric device and circuit that controls a disconnecting means through a relay or equivalent device.
records.gist: A device that opens a remote disconnect through a control relay has a defined term. The question describes it and asks the name.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: disconnecting means. Start with Definition 100, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A disconnecting means is simply the switch or breaker a worker opens before touching equipment. The golden rule is 'within sight': visible and no more than 50 ft away, so nobody can re-energize it unseen. Motors need a disconnect in sight of both the controller and the motor itself; appliances and AC units need one in sight and quickly reachable. If the disconnect must live far away, it has to be lockable open with the location marked on the equipment.

This asks about the disconnect for this equipment. Subject: disconnecting means. Decide whether the question wants its location, its height, its rating, or who may access it.

LOOKUP FOCUS
disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
Article 100 Definitions — Remote Disconnect Control
Remote Disconnect Control. An electric device and circuit that controls a disconnecting means through a relay or equivalent device. (645) (CMP—12)
records.tip_short: Remote Disconnect Control is the device and circuit that works a disconnect through a relay, used in IT rooms. Correct: A — Remote Disconnect Control. Article 100 defines Remote Disconnect Control as a device and circuit controlling a disconnect via relay. Not B: A safety switch is a manually operated enclosed disconnect, not a relay control circuit. Not C: A knife switch is a manual blade switch, not a relay-operated control circuit. Not D: A shunt trip is a breaker accessory that trips it, not the defined control device and circuit.
choice_notes: Article 100 defines Remote Disconnect Control as a device and circuit controlling a disconnect via relay.
A safety switch is a manually operated enclosed disconnect, not a relay control circuit.
A knife switch is a manual blade switch, not a relay-operated control circuit.
A shunt trip is a breaker accessory that trips it, not the defined control device and circuit.

225.19(D)(1) and 225.19(D)(3)
225.19(D)(1) Clearance From Windows
Final spans to the building they supply, or from which they are fed, shall be permitted to be attached to the building, but they shall be kept not less than 900 mm (3 ft) from windows that are designed to be opened, and from doors, porches, balconies, ladders, stairs, fire escapes, or similar locations.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.prompt: A circuit contains two 2,000 ohm resistors connected in parallel. What is the total resistance of the circuit?

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one (two 2,000-ohm resistors = 1,000 ohms). Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s, so 90° takes a quarter of that — 1/240 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

records.reference_text:
310.14(A)(3) Temperature Limitation of Conductors
No conductor shall be used in such a manner that its operating temperature exceeds that designated for the type of insulated conductor involved. In no case shall conductors be associated together in such a way, with respect to type of circuit, the wiring method employed, or the number of conductors, that the limiting temperature of any conductor is exceeded.
Informational Note No. 1: See Table 310.4(1) and Table 315.10(A) for the temperature rating of a conductor that is the maximum temperature, at any location along its length, that the conductor can withstand over a prolonged time period without serious degradation. The ampacity tables of Article 310 and the ampacity tables of Informative Annex B, the ambient temperature correction factors in 310.15(B), and the notes to the tables provide guidance for coordinating conductor sizes, types, ampacities, ambient temperatures, and number of associated conductors. The principal determinants of operating temperature are as follows:
(1) Ambient temperature - ambient temperature may vary along the conductor length as well as from time to time.
(2) Heat generated internally in the conductor as the result of load current flow, including fundamental and harmonic currents.
(3) The rate at which generated heat dissipates into the ambient medium. Thermal insulation that covers or surrounds conductors affects the rate of heat dissipation.
(4) Adjacent load-carrying conductors - adjacent conductors have the dual effect of raising the ambient temperature and impeding heat dissipation.
Informational Note No. 2: Refer to 110.14(C) for the temperature limitation of terminations.

records.prompt: How many apprentice fire alarm installers can be supervised at one time by a license holder?

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
The Nebraska State Electrical Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2101 to 81-2144) decides who may do electrical work for another person. An apprentice registers with the State Electrical Board to learn the trade and may only work under a licensee on the same project.

This asks for a supervision limit set by state law, not by the NEC. Find who may supervise fire alarm apprentices, then the ratio the Act sets for every licensee.

LOOKUP FOCUS

records.reference_text:
81-2108(2) and 81-2113(2) Fire Alarm Installer Supervision; Apprentice Ratio
81-2108(2) Except as provided in section 81-2106, 81-2112, or 81-2144 no person shall wire for or install electrical wiring, apparatus, or equipment or supervise an apprentice electrician unless such person is licensed as a Class B journeyman electrician, a journeyman electrician, a residential journeyman electrician, or a fire alarm installer and is employed by a Class B electrical contractor, an electrical contractor, a Class A master electrician, or a fire alarm installer.
For purposes of this section, the holder of a fire alarm installer license shall only supervise those apprentices engaged in the installation of fire alarm equipment and apparatus operating at fifty volts or less.
81-2113(2) An apprentice electrician shall do no electrical wiring except under the direct personal on-the-job supervision and control and in the immediate presence of a licensee under the State Electrical Act. Such supervision shall include both on-the-job training and related classroom training as approved by the board. The licensee may employ or supervise apprentice electricians at a ratio not to exceed three apprentice electricians to one licensee, except that such ratio and the other requirements of this section shall not be applicable to a teacher-student relationship within a classroom of a community college.

It is the responsibility of the installer or electrical contractor to notify the inspector at such times as the project is ready for inspection. ...
